nit: ideally this would be 'psu-sensor:' at the beginning.
Certainly, but may I confirm, should it be prefixed with `psu-sensor` instead of `pwm-sensor`?
Sorry, `pwm-sensor` as you said.  I mis-typed.  My point was to add an identifier as to which piece of code this is touching.
I understand and have corrected it, thank you for the reminder.

I'm a little confused at this.  This is PWM, ie the current output.  waiting for a fan to physically adjust it's speed would be reflected in RPM, the PWM would apply almost immediately.

Can you clarify in your commit message what this means?  Are we waiting for the actual i2c write?  Doesn't that happen in the actual write call?

Some fan control chips have a [programmable] ramp time so that you're not immediately shifting fans from 0 to 100.  This can be important both for acoustic reasons and for current draw reasons.  It might be difficult for your VR to supply the sudden need for additional current necessary for ramping the fans up rapidly.

The MAX31790 datasheet talks about this:

> Because the duty cycle
> ramps to new values at a controlled rate, the values
> in the two registers can be different. See the Register
> Descriptions section for 

This can mean, as Eric wrote, that the "Desired Target PWM" and the "Currently Driven PWM" can be different.

Definitely. This is what I was trying to explain earlier, but rephrased better. It is clear we need to distinguish between the achieved setting (comes from the hardware) versus the desired setting (comes from the user).
Done
This flow is a little bit confusing.  Does the first operation fail?

No, nothing fails from a BMC perspective.  The phosphor-pid-control won't write the PWM (via dbus-sensors) because it sees that the "Currently Driven PWM" matches its desired PWM target, but if the chip is in the middle of a ramp, this "Currently Driven" doesn't match the "Desired Target".  It causes phosphor-pid-control to miss setting the fans.
Yep, you got it. This is another good reason why we need to have visibility into both of them, because they won't always match each other.
ACK, that makes sense.
Done
Thans for the detailed commit message, Eric!  This is great context.

I am uncertain if this refinement aligns with OpenBMC's definitions and expectations for the `Target` property in the PWM control interface and the `Value` property in the PWM sensor interface.

Additionally, I am unsure if this approach is preferable to implementing driver-specific behaviors within the D-Bus sensor to address the issue.
For instance, handling drivers like [max31790] differently, where the `fan_target` file represents the desired RPM speed instead of PWM.
To calculate the target PWM from the fan_target file, knowledge of the maximum fan tach RPM is required for the conversion.
It's important to consider that the interpretation of sysfs filenames and semantics might differ across drivers, affecting the meanings and relationships of `fan_target` and pwm files.

If there is any guidance or feedback to help determine which method is more appropriate, it would be greatly appreciated.
Thank you very much!

[max31790]: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/a33b5a08cbbdd7aadff95f40cbb45ab86841679e/Documentation/hwmon/max31790.rst#L2

Your insights would be greatly appreciated.

Understood. The reason for removing `setValue` was that I believed it necessary to differentiate the nature of the Control::Target and Sensor::Value properties.
However, if it's deemed more appropriate, I can reinstate the call to `setValue`.

The main goal of this commit is to prevent the Control::Target from being directly tied to changes in the driver PWM file, ensuring that it reflects only the value that the user has explicitly written to the D-Bus interface.
May I clarify, does this imply that if we use the Senosr::Value to control the PWM, the Control::Target should also adjust accordingly to reflect the change?

> May I clarify, does this imply that if we use the Senosr::Value to control the PWM, the Control::Target should also adjust accordingly to reflect the change?

I'm happy to make suggestions, but I'm not really sure what you're trying to accomplish.
busctl set-property ... Target 10
busctl set-property ... Target 100
busctl set-property ... Target 10


I would expect to work based on the existing code, does it not?

I have replicated and verified this issue using such consecutive set-property commands.
On a system with the max31790 driver, when executing these commands with the existing code, setting the `Target` to 100 triggers a get `Target` by the PWM sensor.

However, since the max31790 PWM file still reflects 10, the fan sensor updates the `Target` back to 10.
When the `Target` is set to 10 again, it is skipped because it is perceived as unchanged, resulting in the fan PWM actually being set to 100.
Why does the Target 'get' call do anything with the driver?  This is surprising to me.

My initial intent was to centralize all interactions with the driver PWM file under the Control::Target.
As part of that design, I implemented a recovery check on the driver PWM file during the get operation.

However, I now understand that this approach may not be appropriate, so I will remove it.

This is a great idea. I have long been in favor of having more than one readout, one for the user-desired setting, versus another for the hardware-actual setting. The reason is that of fan lag, as you mentioned, and other things such as sensor value quantization. I thought there was an open GitHub issue for this feature request, but there wasn't. It's a good idea. Thanks for adding it.

I hope someone can continue to provide feedback or merge this commit.
For systems using the MAX31790, the absence of this commit will prevent the fans from being controlled as expected, which may lead to inaccurate fan-related events or even overheating issues.

> I thought there was an open GitHub issue for this feature request, but there wasn't

There was indeed one issue since 2023 directly related to this issue (https://github.com/openbmc/dbus-sensors/issues/25).

Although we internally chose to modify the max31790 driver to show the user-requested PWM in pwm* file (show MAX31790_REG_PWMOUT register value instead of MAX31790_REG_PWM_DUTY_CYCLE, because pwm* is for setting the desired PWM to the fan, we think it should show back the value we set) as a WA for this issue, I think it can be closed with this patch.
Thank you very much for sharing your experience.

I prefer this over Gerrit 82199.

When it comes to phosphor-fan-presence repo, phosphor-fan-monitor service compares between Target and Value for a configured period of time to see if Value lies within the allowed range computed from Target and a set of offset, deviation, ... This is to ensure that the physical fans are running at the desired speed set to Target by phosphor-fan-control service. If this check fails, Functional property is set to false for fan inventory objects under phosphor-inventory-manager => fan fault LED might be turned ON.

If both Value and Target show hardware value, this check will never fail. So separate implementations of the two can better adhere to their names and help in those monitoring practices.

Hi @patrick@stwcx.xyz, since this commit has been pending for quite a while, do you have any additional feedback or changes you’d like me to make?
Thank you very much.
I don't have any additional feedback.  Please mark the comments resolved if you agree with going this direction and not 82199.

Okay, I have marked the other unresolved comments as resolved.
Thank you.

This brought up another question. The purpose of `Target` versus `Value` is subtle. I think, but am not entirely sure, that there were 3 reasons:
* `Target` is integer, from 0 to 255, so it easily maintains a 1:1 correspondence to the underlying Linux kernel `hwmon` interface (for fan PWM).
* Being an integer, it can always be easily compared for equality without floating-point loss, which is important for the optimization of avoiding duplicate settings if the setting already matches what was desired.
* `Target` is always read/write, versus `Value` which was always read-only until late 2021 when the `ValueMutability` feature landed.

Other than these, the `Target` value is interchangeable with `Value`, IIRC. They update each other, in lockstep. Changing one, always and instantly, will change the other. At least that's how it's been, in my experience, for fan PWM.

To change the meaning of `Target` or `Value` now, to have it reflect the delayed response from the hardware instead of the user's instantaneous desired intent, might have other side effects. We might need a third field. However, this would require an interface change. The advantage of adding a third field is that it would help disambiguate all of this historical baggage, and it would help greatly for user-settable sensors, to avoid the race condition between the desired setting (flowing down from user to hardware), and the actual value (flowing up from hardware to user).

Would it make sense to try the following approach:
Keep `Target` and `Value` interchangeable as before, and add a new read/write D-Bus property that explicitly stores `user intent`.

This property would serve as the canonical reference for write decisions (i.e., when a PWM write is requested via any property, the incoming value is compared against the last recorded `user intent` to decide whether to write to hardware).

This way, any of the three properties could trigger a PWM write, but the write-decision logic would always compare the incoming value against the last recorded `user intent`, rather than against the current `Value` or `Target`.

Separately, I noticed [Gerrit 82199] takes a more direct approach to fix this issue, but it introduces additional reads of the hardware PWM file and does not rely on the D-Bus property to decide whether to write to hardware.

I’d appreciate additional feedback from reviewers on which direction is preferred.

[Gerrit 82199]: https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/dbus-sensors/+/82199

So in case of `- Delayed Reflection Drivers (e.g., max31790)`
we can set `Value` property (which is meaningless, since we do not control the currently driven PWM) and it then goes ahead to set `Target` property.

@eric.yang.wiwynn@gmail.com
Why would a caller not directly set `Target` property?

The `Sensor.Value` interface is documented to be read-only.

> All Sensor.Value properties are read-only.

https://github.com/openbmc/phosphor-dbus-interfaces/blob/master/yaml/xyz/openbmc_project/Sensor/Value.interface.yaml

I originally thought that users could control the PWM simply by setting the `Target` property.
However, [discussions in the comments of Patchset 4] suggested that we should retain the original functionality of setting the PWM via the `Value` property as well.
Additionally, I'm not sure whether other parts of the OpenBMC codebase set the PWM through the `Value` property.
Moreover, I need `Target` to reflect the user’s intended PWM value in order to address the issue this patch is meant to solve.
That’s why I implemented this by calling the set `Target` property method here.

Regardless of whether setting the `Value` property also sets the PWM, this does not affect resolving issues such as the `Delayed Reflection Drivers` problem, as long as the `Target` property always reflects the user's intent and does not change according to the actual PWM file value from the driver.

[discussions in the comments of Patchset 4]: https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/dbus-sensors/+/79824/comment/51cb8408_c5930df4/

> suggested that we should retain the original functionality of setting the PWM via the Value property as well.

The `Sensor.Value` interface is documented to be read-only and it has been that way ever since the interface was first documented in the PDI in 2016.

It's a Sensor, reading a value. There is no sense in writing to it. Conceptually it does not make any sense (at least not to me).

@patrick@stwcx.xyz Should we update the yaml on `Sensor.Value` to clarify that it is also meant as a writable control interface in some cases?

Otherwise we could probably add a big 
```lg2::error("Writing to a read-only sensor interface")```
statement into the setter there and leave it there for a while to see if anything actually uses the interface in that way.

Careful, because since we updated it in 2021, the `Sensor.Value` field can also be read/write, if it is mutable. See the `ValueMutability` interface here: https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/phosphor-dbus-interfaces/+/36333

The implementation is in https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/dbus-sensors/+/45405 and a user of this feature, the IPMI server, is here: https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/phosphor-host-ipmid/+/45407

Here's where the IPMI sensor performs the write: https://github.com/openbmc/phosphor-host-ipmid/blob/master/dbus-sdr/sensorcommands.cpp#L831-L833

I wonder if we should update the YAML documentation for `Sensor.Value` to show that it is read/write in some situations, but read-only in most situations? Not sure how to indicate that the permissions are contingent on something else (in this case the `ValueMutability.Mutable` setting).

> I wonder if we should update the YAML documentation for Sensor.Value to show that it is read/write in some situations, but read-only in most situations?

Raised https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/phosphor-dbus-interfaces/+/82110,
please review.

I don't think that's something the yaml or the generated code currently supports.

> and a user of this feature, the IPMI server, is here

good to know at least someone here has an overview 😊

Thanks! Reviewed it.

FYI, I also tried to find the equivalent sensor write handler in the Redfish server, `bmcweb`, but did not find it after a quick look. I'm pretty sure this feature exists already, it might have been in a local patch? Regardless, the `ValueMutability` interface is intended for any situation in which there's a sensor write request coming in from an external source and we need to validate if it's allowed or not.

The important thing here is that `Value` can be written to, just like `Target`, and there's really no prohibition on the user doing so, if they have permission, so we have to handle these equivalently. I wonder if we should add additional fields, perhaps `IntendedValue` and/or `HardwareValue`, to disambiguate?

Maybe i am not getting the big picture here, but do we actually need a Pwm `Sensor`?

The PID loop is taking temperatures and adjusting the pwm value to control the fan speed.

If the fan speed is not reaching the requested value after some time then that's an error condition.

Since the pwm is a control input which is assumed to just 'work' if correctly configured. So we should be able to assume it always has the correct value?

Looked into the `max31790` datasheet and there they mention the delay to reflection can be up to `125ms` which i would consider to be a minor delay and probably nothing to worry about in the control loop.

Since the PwmSensor looks like the interface boundary between the sysfs and the PID loop, can we just shortcut the implementation to store the pwm value internally anytime the user sets it and return that if requested?

If there is anything bypassing the PwmSensor, that's broken anyways?

Another point: concepts like 'Threshold' do not make sense for a control input.

Would it be preferable to avoid making the `Target` property reflect pure “user intent,” and instead keep the user intent as an internal variable used to decide whether to write to the hardware?
This would keep the external properties aligned with the actual hardware PWM value while still preserving intent internally for comparison.

Separately, I reviewed [Gerrit 82199].
It addresses inconsistencies by re-reading the hardware PWM in the setters and updating only when the hardware differs.
That should also solve this issue, but it does increase reads of the hardware PWM file.

@patrick@stwcx.xyz, could you kindly share your thoughts or preference?

[Gerrit 82199]: https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/dbus-sensors/+/82199

I prefer this over [Gerrit 82199](https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/dbus-sensors/+/82199).

When it comes to phosphor-fan-presence repo, phosphor-fan-monitor service compares between `Target` and `Value` for a configured period of time to see if `Value` lies within the allowed range computed from `Target` and a set of offset, deviation, ... This is to ensure that the physical fans are running at the desired speed set to `Target` by phosphor-fan-control service. If this check fails, `Functional` property is set to false for fan inventory objects under phosphor-inventory-manager => fan fault LED might be turned ON.

If both `Value` and `Target` show hardware value, this check will never fail. So separate implementations of the two can better adhere to their names and help in those monitoring practices.

To double check, if I intentionally set 255 to a fan that was previously controlled to be running at 150, `Value` will show the new speed and `Target` will still show 150/255, right?

Thank you for your feedback and support.

If you mean a fan whose `Target` was set to 150, and the PWM is changed to 255 via the driver or an I2C command, then `Value` will show 100% (the new hardware PWM 255) while `Target` will still show 150.

In other words, only the `Value` follows the hardware value reported by the driver; the `Target` only changes when the user sets it via D-Bus.

> If you mean a fan whose Target was set to 150, and the PWM is changed to 255 via the driver or an I2C command, then Value will show 100% (the new hardware PWM 255) while Target will still show 150.

Yes that's what I meant.

> In other words, only the Value follows the hardware value reported by the driver; the Target only changes when the user sets it via D-Bus.

As expected. Thanks.
